sources.filename: Republic Act No. 11199 (Social Security Act of 2018)
sources.notes: Approved 7 February 2019; consolidation of Senate Bill No. 1753 and House Bill No. 2158 passed 28 November 2018. Repeals RA 1161 and RA 8282. All section verbatims in this fragment are quoted from this text (obvious encoding/OCR artifacts normalized). Official Gazette endpoint returned HTTP 403 on the access date, so Lawphil is the retrievable host.

Current tables effective January 2025, implementing the final step of the RA 11199 Sec. 4(a)(9) schedule: SSS Circulars No. 2024-006 (employer/employee), 2024-007 (household employer/kasambahay), 2024-008 (self-employed), 2024-009 (voluntary/non-working spouse), 2024-010 (land-based OFW). Still the latest table published on sss.gov.ph as of the access date; no 2026 schedule had been posted.

sources.filename: SSS: Pay Contributions (contribution rules by member class)
sources.notes: Confirms 15% of MSC (max P35,000), employer 10.0% / employee 5.0%, effective 1 January 2025; MSC range P5,000-P35,000 with MSC above P20,000 credited to the MPF (MySSS Pension Booster); EC P10/P30 (since 1 January 2007), SE under ECP since September 2020 (ECC-SSS JMC No. 1, s. 2020); land-based OFW minimum MSC P8,000; non-working-spouse MSC from 50% of working spouse income; age-55 MSC-change limits for SE/VM/OFW.

sources.filename: SSS: Funeral Benefit (current amounts and conditions)
sources.notes: Current rule: variable P20,000-P60,000 if the member paid at least 36 contributions; fixed P12,000 if at least 1 but fewer than 36. Per SSS Circular No. 2023-009 (Revised Guidelines on the Funeral Benefit Program), effective 20 October 2023, per PIA announcement of the SSS release.

sources.filename: SSS: Maternity Benefit (Expanded Maternity Leave Law rules)
sources.notes: RA 11210 (105-Day Expanded Maternity Leave Law) rules apply to contingencies on or after 11 March 2019: 105 days live childbirth (normal or caesarian), 60 days miscarriage/ETP including stillbirth, 120 days for solo parents (105+15); every instance regardless of frequency; 100% of ADSC; at least 3 monthly contributions in the 12-month period preceding the semester of contingency; employer advances within 30 days, SSS reimburses 100%.

sources.filename: SSS: Unemployment Benefit (qualifying conditions and procedure)
sources.notes: Mirrors Sec. 14-B (not over 60; at least 36 contributions with 12 in the 18-month period before involuntary separation; once every 3 years) plus current procedure: claim within 1 year of separation, DOLE electronic Certification of Involuntary Separation (apply within 30 days of online SSS filing), just-cause separations under Labor Code Art. 297 excluded.

sources.filename: SSS v. Aguas, G.R. No. 165546, 27 February 2006
sources.publisher: Supreme Court of the Philippines (via Lawphil)
sources.notes: Death-benefits case: surviving-spouse primary-beneficiary test (legitimate spouse AND dependent for support); dependency is not presumed from marriage alone. Petition partially granted; only Jeylnn declared entitled. E-Library mirror: thebookshelf/showdocs/1/41086.

sources.filename: Ortega v. SSC, G.R. No. 176150, 25 June 2008 (578 Phil. 338)
sources.publisher: Supreme Court of the Philippines (via Lawphil)
sources.notes: Disability case: SSC/CA denial of total permanent disability affirmed; SSS benefits vs Labor Code compensation are distinct in nature and purpose; SSC findings stand on substantial evidence. E-Library mirror: thebookshelf/showdocs/1/45458.

sources.filename: Ambassador Hotel v. SSS, G.R. No. 194137, 21 June 2017 (811 Phil. 424)
sources.publisher: Supreme Court of the Philippines (via Lawphil)
sources.notes: Employer-liability case: SSS remittance is mandatory; corporation liable though officers bear criminal responsibility (Sec. 28(f)); arrest of managing head gives jurisdiction over the corporation; officer acquittal does not extinguish corporate civil liability (P584,804.00 + 6% legal interest). E-Library mirror: thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63118.

sources.filename: Gapayao v. Fulo, G.R. No. 193493, 13 June 2013
sources.publisher: Supreme Court of the Philippines (via Lawphil)
sources.notes: Coverage case: compulsory SSS coverage follows the employer-employee relationship under the control test (right to control suffices; pakyaw workers are employees); factual findings of the SSC affirmed by the CA are final on substantial evidence; unreported worker's death triggers Sec. 24(a) damages. E-Library mirror: thebookshelf/showdocs/1/56031.

provisions.verbatim: Employer — Any person, natural or juridical, domestic or foreign, who carries on in the Philippines any trade, business, industry, undertaking, or activity of any kind and uses the services of another person who is under his orders as regards the employment, except the government and any of its political subdivisions, branches or instrumentalities, including corporations owned or controlled by the Government: Provided, That a self-employed person shall be both employee and employer at the same time.
provisions.explanation: An employer is anyone running any trade or activity in the Philippines who uses another person's services under his orders. The government and its branches, subdivisions, instrumentalities, and GOCCs are excluded (their workers fall under the GSIS, not the SSS). The proviso matters for payroll thinking: a self-employed person wears both hats, so he shoulders both the employer and employee shares of the contribution. Remember: coverage follows the employment relationship — no employer-employee relationship, no compulsory coverage as employee (see Sec. 8(j)(1) and Gapayao v. Fulo).

provisions.verbatim: Employee — Any person who performs services for an employer in which either or both mental or physical efforts are used and who receives compensation for such services, where there is an employer-employee relationship: Provided, That a self-employed person shall be both employee and employer at the same time.
provisions.explanation: An employee is one who renders service (mental or physical) for compensation within an employer-employee relationship. For accountancy students: when classifying workers for SSS payroll compliance, apply the labor-law control test — the person for whom services are performed must have the right to control both the end and the manner and means (Gapayao). Job title, pakyaw/piece-rate pay, or irregular hours do not by themselves defeat employee status. Remember: a self-employed person is deemed both employee and employer, so he pays both shares.

provisions.verbatim: Employment — Any service performed by an employee for his employer except: (1) Services where there is no employer-employee relationship in accordance with existing labor laws, rules, regulations and jurisprudence; (2) Service performed in the employ of the Philippine Government or instrumentality or agency thereof; (3) Service performed in the employ of a foreign government or international organization, or their wholly-owned instrumentality: Provided, however, That this exemption notwithstanding, any foreign government, international organization or their wholly-owned instrumentality employing workers in the Philippines or employing Filipinos outside of the Philippines, may enter into an agreement with the Philippine Government for the inclusion of such employees in the SSS except those already covered by their respective civil service retirement systems: Provided, further, That the terms of such agreement shall conform with the provisions of this Act on coverage and amount of payment of contributions and benefits: Provided, finally, That the provisions of this Act shall be supplementary to any such agreement; and (4) Such other services performed by temporary and other employees which may be excluded by regulation of the Commission. Employees of bona fide independent contractors shall not be deemed employees of the employer engaging the service of said contractors.
provisions.explanation: Employment means covered service, minus four exclusions: (1) no employer-employee relationship (genuine independent contractors are out — but their own employees are covered as employees of the contractor); (2) Philippine government service (GSIS territory); (3) foreign government/international-organization service, unless brought in by agreement; (4) services the Commission excludes by regulation. Practical application: before enrolling a worker, HR/payroll must first settle whether he is an employee or a bona fide contractor's employee. Exam point: memorize the four exclusions — questions often test whether a government worker, a contractor's crew, or an embassy hire is compulsorily covered.

provisions.verbatim: Member — The worker who is covered under Section 9, Section 9-A and Section 9-B of this Act.
provisions.explanation: A member is simply a worker covered under any of the three coverage sections: employees (Sec. 9), self-employed (Sec. 9-A), and OFWs (Sec. 9-B). Every benefit provision that says 'a member' presupposes this status. Remember: voluntary members (non-working spouses, separated members who continue paying, permanent migrants) keep member status through continued coverage, not through a separate definition.

provisions.verbatim: Self-employed — Any person whose income is not derived from employment, as defined under this Act, as well as those workers enumerated in Section 9-A hereof.
provisions.explanation: Self-employed captures everyone whose income does not come from employment, plus the enumerated workers in Sec. 9-A (professionals, single proprietors and partners, actors/directors/scriptwriters/correspondents who are not employees, athletes/coaches/trainers/jockeys, farmers and fishermen). For compliance: these members register themselves, declare their monthly earnings, and pay both shares. Exam point: 'income not derived from employment' is the general test; the Sec. 9-A enumeration is expressly non-exclusive ('including, but not limited to').

provisions.verbatim: (a) Coverage in the SSS shall be compulsory upon all employees including kasambahays or domestic workers not over sixty (60) years of age and their employers: Provided, That any benefit already earned by the employees under private benefit plans existing at the time of the approval of this Act shall not be discontinued, reduced or otherwise impaired: Provided, further, That private plans which are existing and in force at the time of compulsory coverage shall be integrated with the plan of the SSS in such a way where the employer's contribution to his private plan is more than that required of him in this Act, he shall pay to the SSS only the contribution required of him and he shall continue his contribution to such private plan less his contribution to the SSS so that the employer's total contribution to his benefit plan and to the SSS shall be the same as his contribution to his private benefit plan before the compulsory coverage: Provided, further, That any changes, adjustments, modifications, eliminations or improvements in the benefits to be available under the remaining private plan, which may be necessary to adopt by reason of the reduced contributions thereto as a result of the integration, shall be subject to agreements between the employers and employees concerned: Provided, further, That the private benefit plan which the employer shall continue for his employees shall remain under the employer's management and control unless there is an existing agreement to the contrary: Provided, finally, That nothing in this Act shall be construed as a limitation on the right of employers and employees to agree on and adopt benefits which are over and above those provided under this Act. (b) Spouses who devote full time to managing the household and family affairs, unless they are also engaged in other vocation or employment which is subject to mandatory coverage, may be covered by the SSS on a voluntary basis.
provisions.explanation: Paragraph (a) states the core compulsory-coverage rule: every employee not over 60 — expressly including kasambahays and domestic workers — plus their employers. The provisos protect existing private plans: earned benefits cannot be cut, employer contributions integrate (SSS first, the balance stays with the private plan, total cost unchanged), adjustments need employer-employee agreement, and parties may always agree on benefits above the SSS floor. Paragraph (b) creates the non-working-spouse voluntary track: full-time homemakers may join voluntarily, unless they are already mandatorily covered by other work. Practical application: household employers must register kasambahays (current schedule: SSS Circular No. 2024-007, eff. 1 Jan 2025); payroll officers must never treat a private retirement plan as a substitute for SSS coverage. Remember: 'not over 60' is the age ceiling for compulsory employee coverage.

provisions.verbatim: Compulsory Coverage of the Self-Employed. — Coverage in the SSS shall also be compulsory upon such self-employed persons as may be determined by the Commission under such rules and regulations as it may prescribe, including, but not limited to the following: (a) All self-employed professionals; (b) Partners and single proprietors of businesses; (c) Actors and actresses, directors, scriptwriters and news correspondents who do not fall within the definition of the term 'employee' in Section 8(d) of this Act; (d) Professional athletes, coaches, trainers and jockeys; and (e) Individual farmers and fishermen. Unless otherwise specified herein, all provisions of this Act applicable to covered employees shall also be applicable to the covered self-employed persons.
provisions.explanation: Self-employed coverage is compulsory, not optional — the Commission only fills in the mechanics. The enumeration (professionals, partners and single proprietors, listed media/sports workers who are not employees, individual farmers and fishermen) is expressly non-exhaustive. The closing sentence is the workhorse: everything applicable to covered employees applies to covered self-employed persons unless the Act says otherwise. Practical application: a CPA in independent practice, a sari-sari store owner, and a tricycle operator are all compulsorily covered and pay both shares on declared earnings. Remember: freelancers who ARE employees of a client (control test) fall under Sec. 9, not Sec. 9-A.

provisions.verbatim: Compulsory Coverage of Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) — (a) Coverage in the SSS shall be compulsory upon all sea-based and land-based OFWs as defined under Republic Act No. 8042, otherwise known as the Migrant Workers and Overseas Filipinos Act of 1995, as amended by Republic Act No. 10022: Provided, That they are not over sixty (60) years of age. All benefit provisions under this Act shall apply to all covered OFWs. The benefits include, among others, retirement, death, disability, funeral, sickness and maternity. (b) Manning agencies are agents of their principals and are considered as employers of sea-based OFWs. For purposes of the implementation of this Act, any law to the contrary notwithstanding manning agencies are jointly and severally or solidarity liable with their principals with respect to the civil liabilities incurred for any violation of this Act. The persons having direct control, management or direction of the manning agencies shall be held criminally liable for any act or omission penalized under this Act notwithstanding Section 28(f) hereof. (c) Land-based OFWs are compulsory members of the SSS and considered in the same manner as self-employed persons under such rules and regulations that the Commission shall prescribe. (d) The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) and all its agencies involved in deploying OFWs for employment abroad are mandated to negotiate bilateral labor agreements with the OFWs' host countries to ensure that the employers of land-based OFWs, similar to the principals of sea-based OFWs, pay the required SSS contributions, in which case these land-based OFWs shall no longer be considered in the same manner as self-employed persons in this Act. Instead, they shall be considered as compulsorily covered employees with employer and employee shares in contributions that shall be provided for in the bilateral labor agreements and their implementing administrative agreements: Provided, That in countries which already extend social security coverage to OFWs, the DFA through the Philippine embassies and the DOLE shall negotiate further agreements to serve the best interests of the OFWs. (e) The DFA, the DOLE and the SSS shall ensure compulsory coverage of OFWs through bilateral social security and labor agreements and other measures for enforcement. (f) Upon the termination of their employment overseas, OFWs may continue to pay contributions on a voluntary basis to maintain their rights to full benefits. (g) Filipino permanent migrants, including Filipino immigrants, permanent residents and naturalized citizens of their host countries may be covered by the SSS on a voluntary basis.
provisions.explanation: RA 11199 made OFW coverage compulsory — the single biggest coverage expansion of the 2018 rewrite. Sea-based OFWs are treated as employees of their manning agencies, which are solidarily liable with foreign principals for civil liabilities, while the agency's controlling persons face criminal liability. Land-based OFWs are currently treated as self-employed (minimum MSC P8,000 under current SSS rules) until bilateral agreements shift their foreign employers into the employer-share role. Paragraphs (f) and (g) create two voluntary tracks: separated OFWs who keep paying, and permanent migrants. Practical application: manning agencies must remit like any employer; a land-based OFW budgets for both shares. Exam points: (1) OFW age ceiling is also 'not over 60'; (2) manning-agency solidary liability; (3) land-based OFW = self-employed treatment is the default rule, bilateral-agreement employee treatment the exception.

provisions.verbatim: Effective Date of Coverage. — Compulsory coverage of the employer shall take effect on the first day of his operation and that of the employee on the day of his employment: Provided, That the compulsory coverage of the self-employed person shall take effect upon his registration with the SSS.
provisions.explanation: Three effectivity triggers: the employer is covered from the first day of business operations; the employee from day one of employment (no probation or regularization requirement); the self-employed person only upon registration with the SSS. Practical application: a newly hired employee is already covered on his first day of work, so payroll must deduct from the first payroll period, and the employer must report him immediately (Sec. 24(a)) — delay risks damages if a contingency strikes. Remember the triplet: operation / employment / registration.

provisions.verbatim: Effect of Separation from Employment. — When an employee under compulsory coverage is separated from employment, his employer's contribution on his account and his obligation to pay contributions arising from that employment shall cease at the end of the month of separation, but said employee shall be credited with all contributions paid on his behalf and entitled to benefits according to the provisions of this Act. He may, however, continue to pay the total contributions to maintain his right to full benefit.
provisions.explanation: Separation ends the contribution obligation at the end of the month of separation — but never wipes the slate: all paid contributions stay credited and benefit rights survive. The separated employee may keep paying the total contribution (both shares) as a voluntary member to preserve full benefit rights. Practical application: resigned or retired employees deciding whether to continue paying should weigh the qualifying-contribution thresholds (120 for retirement pension, 36 for death/disability pension, 3 for sickness/maternity) against the voluntary cost. Remember: 'credited with all contributions' — SSS membership has no forfeiture of paid contributions.

provisions.verbatim: Effect of Interruption of Business or Professional Income. — If the self-employed member realizes no income in any given month, he shall not be required to pay contributions for that month. He may, however, be allowed to continue paying contributions under the same rules and regulations applicable to a separated employee member: Provided, That no retroactive payment of contributions shall be allowed other than as prescribed under Section 22-A hereof.
provisions.explanation: A self-employed member with zero income in a month is excused from paying for that month — the counterpart of Sec. 11 for employees. He may still pay voluntarily under the separated-employee rules, but he cannot later backfill skipped months (no retroactive payment, except as Sec. 22-A allows). Practical application: seasonal earners (farmers, fishermen, project-based professionals) should plan voluntary payments around the benefit-qualifying windows rather than assuming they can catch up later. Exam point: pair Sec. 11-A with Sec. 22-A (quarterly SE remittance, no retroactive payment).

provisions.verbatim: Dependents — The dependents shall be the following: (1) The legal spouse entitled by law to receive support from the member; (2) The legitimate, legitimated or legally adopted, and illegitimate child who is unmarried, not gainfully employed, and has not reached twenty-one (21) years of age, or if over twenty-one (21) years of age, he is congenitally or while still a minor has been permanently incapacitated and incapable of self-support, physically or mentally; and (3) The parent who is receiving regular support from the member.
provisions.explanation: Dependents are a closed list: the legal spouse entitled to support, each qualifying child (legitimate, legitimated, legally adopted, or illegitimate — unmarried, not gainfully employed, under 21, or incapacitated since minority), and a parent receiving regular support. This definition feeds the dependents' pension (Sec. 12-A) and the beneficiary ladder (Sec. 8(k)). Practical application: HR dependent declarations and SSS beneficiary records must be kept current — an unreported dependent cannot draw a dependents' pension. Exam point: illegitimate children ARE dependents and can be primary beneficiaries, but at 50% of a legitimate child's share when legitimate children exist (Sec. 8(k)).

provisions.verbatim: Beneficiaries — The dependent spouse until he or she remarries, the dependent legitimate, legitimated or legally adopted, and illegitimate children, who shall be the primary beneficiaries of the member: Provided, That the dependent illegitimate children shall be entitled to fifty percent (50%) of the share of the legitimate, legitimated or legally adopted children: Provided, further, That in the absence of the dependent legitimate, legitimated or legally adopted children of the member, his/her dependent illegitimate children shall be entitled to one hundred percent (100%) of the benefits. In their absence, the dependent parents who shall be the secondary beneficiaries of the member. In the absence of all the foregoing, any other person designated by the member as his/her secondary beneficiary.
provisions.explanation: The beneficiary ladder has three rungs: primary (dependent spouse until remarriage + dependent children), secondary (dependent parents), and designated secondary (any person the member designates, only if no primary or secondary exists). The illegitimate-child sharing rule is heavily tested: 50% of a legitimate child's share when legitimate children concur, 100% when they do not. The spouse's status ends on remarriage. Practical application: members should file and update designations; claims processors apply this ladder strictly in death (Sec. 13) and survivor-pension (Secs. 12-B(d), 13-A(c)) cases. Remember: Aguas adds the dependency proof requirement for the spouse — legitimate marriage alone is not enough.

provisions.verbatim: Average monthly salary credit — The result obtained by dividing the sum of the last sixty (60) monthly salary credits immediately preceding the semester of contingency by sixty (60), or the result obtained by dividing the sum of all the monthly salary credits paid prior to the semester of contingency by the number of monthly contributions paid in the same period, whichever is greater: Provided, That the injury or sickness which caused the disability shall be deemed as the permanent disability for the purpose of computing the average monthly salary credit.
provisions.explanation: The AMSC is the average of the member's monthly salary credits, computed two ways with the HIGHER result controlling: (1) last 60 MSCs before the semester of contingency divided by 60, or (2) all MSCs paid before the semester of contingency divided by the number of contributions. Since the pension formulas (Sec. 12) are percentages of AMSC, higher and more consistent lifetime credits mean higher pensions. Practical application: voluntary members choosing an MSC are effectively choosing their future AMSC inputs — a low declared MSC today depresses the pension base. Remember: always compute both and take the greater.

provisions.verbatim: Monthly Pension. — (a) The monthly pension shall be the highest of the following amounts: (1) The sum of the following: (i) Three hundred pesos (P300.00); plus (ii) Twenty percent (20%) of the average monthly salary credit; plus (iii) Two percent (2%) of the average monthly salary credit for each credited year of service in excess of ten (10) years; or (2) Forty percent (40%) of the average monthly salary credit; or (3) One thousand pesos (P1,000.00): Provided, That the monthly pension shall in no case be paid for an aggregate amount of less than sixty (60) months. (b) Notwithstanding the preceding paragraph, the minimum pension shall be One thousand two hundred pesos (P1,200.00) for members with at least ten (10) credited years of service and Two thousand four hundred pesos (P2,400.00) for those with twenty (20) credited years of service: Provided, That the Commission, upon determination of actuarial soundness, may provide pension increase than the amounts specified herein. (c) Additional Benefit Allowance. — Pursuant to Memorandum from the Executive Secretary dated 22 February 2017, by authority of the President of the Republic of the Philippines, an additional monthly benefit allowance amounting to One thousand pesos (P1,000.00) shall be given to all retirement, death, and disability pensioners receiving monthly pensions in or after January two thousand seventeen (2017). The Commission may determine the grant of additional benefit allowance: Provided, That the actuarial soundness of the reserve fund shall be guaranteed. All other additional allowances to monthly pension subsequent to the Memorandum of the Executive Secretary dated February 22, 2017 shall be subject to the requirement of fund viability and sustainability as determined by the Commission based on the recommendations of the Office of the Chief Actuary guaranteeing the actuarial soundness of the grant of such allowances.
provisions.explanation: The monthly pension is the highest of three computations: (1) P300 + 20% of AMSC + 2% of AMSC per credited year of service beyond 10; (2) 40% of AMSC; or (3) a P1,000 floor — and it is guaranteed for at least 60 months in aggregate (the five-year guarantee that survivor provisions repeatedly invoke). Minimums: P1,200 (at least 10 CYS) and P2,400 (at least 20 CYS). The P1,000 additional allowance dates to January 2017 by executive authority and is codified here; later increases need actuarial soundness. Worked example: AMSC P15,000 with 25 CYS gives formula (1) = 300 + 3,000 + (15 × 300) = P7,800; formula (2) = P6,000; formula (3) = P1,000 — pension is P7,800 (before the allowance). Peso figures are as stated in RA 11199 — verify current pension amounts and any later increases with SSS before relying on them. Exam point: the 60-month guarantee is the bridge to Secs. 12-B(d) and 13-A(c).

provisions.verbatim: Dependents' Pension. — Where monthly pension is payable on account of death, permanent total disability or retirement, dependents' pension equivalent to ten percent (10%) of the monthly pension or Two hundred fifty pesos (P250.00), whichever is higher, shall also be paid for each dependent child conceived on or before the date of the contingency but not exceeding five (5), beginning with the youngest and without substitution: Provided, That where there are legitimate and illegitimate children, the former shall be preferred.
provisions.explanation: Each qualifying dependent child adds 10% of the monthly pension (minimum P250) on top of the retirement, death, or permanent-total-disability pension. Limits: conceived on or before the contingency date, maximum five children, youngest first, no substitution — and legitimate children are preferred over illegitimate ones in filling the five slots. Practical application: a retiree's monthly check is pension + (dependents' pensions), so dependent declarations directly affect the payout; children conceived after the contingency are excluded. Remember: five children max, P250 floor per child, and this add-on attaches only to monthly pensions for death, permanent total disability, or retirement.

provisions.verbatim: Retirement Benefits. — (a) A member who has paid at least one hundred twenty (120) monthly contributions prior to the semester of retirement and who: (1) has reached the age of sixty (60) years and is already separated from employment or has ceased to be self-employed; or (2) has reached the age of sixty-five (65) years, shall be entitled for as long as he lives to the monthly pension: Provided, That he shall have the option to receive his first eighteen (18) monthly pensions in lump sum discounted at a preferential rate of interest to be determined by the SSS. (b) A covered member who is sixty (60) years old at retirement and who does not qualify for pension benefits under paragraph (a) above, shall be entitled to a lump sum benefit equal to the total contributions paid by him and on his behalf: Provided, That he is separated from employment and is not continuing payment of contributions to the SSS on his own. (c) The monthly pension shall be suspended upon the reemployment or resumption of self-employment of a retired member who is less than sixty-five (65) years old. He shall again be subject to Section Eighteen and his employer to Section Nineteen of this Act. (d) Upon the death of the retired member, his primary beneficiaries as of the date of his retirement shall be entitled to receive the monthly pension: Provided, That if he has no primary beneficiaries and he dies within sixty (60) months from the start of his monthly pension, his secondary beneficiaries shall be entitled to a lump sum benefit equivalent to the total monthly pensions corresponding to the balance of the five-year guaranteed period, excluding the dependents' pension. (e) The monthly pension of a member who retires after reaching age sixty (60) shall be the higher of either: (1) the monthly pension computed at the earliest time he could have retired had he been separated from employment or ceased to be self-employed plus all adjustments thereto; or (2) the monthly pension computed at the time when he actually retires.
provisions.explanation: Retirement has two doors: optional at 60 (with 120 contributions AND separation/cessation of self-employment) and mandatory at 65 (120 contributions; separation not required). With 120 contributions the prize is a lifetime monthly pension, with an option to take the first 18 months as a discounted lump sum. At 60 without 120 contributions, the member gets only a lump sum equal to total contributions paid (and must stop paying). Reemployment before 65 suspends the pension and restarts coverage. Death of a retiree passes the monthly pension to primary beneficiaries as of the retirement date; if there are none and death occurs within 60 months, secondary beneficiaries get the balance of the five-year guarantee as a lump sum (excluding dependents' pensions). Late retirees get the higher of the earliest-possible or actual-retirement computation. Practical application: the 120-contribution line is the most important number in retirement planning — voluntary continuation (Sec. 11) exists precisely to cross it. Remember: 60 needs separation, 65 does not.

provisions.verbatim: Death Benefits. — Upon the death of a member who has paid at least thirty-six (36) monthly contributions prior to the semester of death, his primary beneficiaries shall be entitled to the monthly pension: Provided, That if he has no primary beneficiaries, his secondary beneficiaries shall be entitled to a lump sum benefit equivalent to thirty-six (36) times the monthly pension. If he has not paid the required thirty-six (36) monthly contributions, his primary or secondary beneficiaries shall be entitled to a lump sum benefit equivalent to the monthly pension times the number of monthly contributions paid to the SSS or twelve (12) times the monthly pension, whichever is higher.
provisions.explanation: Death benefits turn on two questions: (1) did the member pay at least 36 contributions before the semester of death, and (2) are there primary beneficiaries? With 36+ contributions: primary beneficiaries draw the monthly pension; if none, secondary beneficiaries get a lump sum of 36 × monthly pension. Below 36 contributions: whoever qualifies (primary or secondary) gets a lump sum of (monthly pension × contributions paid) or 12 × monthly pension, whichever is higher. Practical application: claims processors must first count contributions, then apply the Sec. 8(k) ladder as refined by Aguas (spouse must prove dependency; only legitimate, legitimated, legally adopted, or illegitimate children qualify — informal adoptees do not). Remember the ladder: 36+ and primary → pension; 36+ without primary → 36× lump sum; below 36 → contributions× or 12×, higher.

provisions.verbatim: Permanent Disability Benefits. — (a) Upon the permanent total disability of a member who has paid at least thirty-six (36) monthly contributions prior to the semester of disability, he shall be entitled to the monthly pension: Provided, That if he has not paid the required thirty-six (36) monthly contributions, he shall be entitled to a lump sum benefit equivalent to the monthly pension times the number of monthly contributions paid to the SSS or twelve (12) times the monthly pension, whichever is higher. A member who (1) has received a lump sum benefit; and (2) is reemployed or has resumed self-employment not earlier than one (1) year from the date of his disability shall again be subject to compulsory coverage and shall be considered a new member. (b) The monthly pension and dependents' pension shall be suspended upon the reemployment or resumption of self-employment or the recovery of the disabled member from his permanent total disability or his failure to present himself for examination at least once a year upon notice by the SSS. (c) Upon the death of the permanent total disability pensioner, his primary beneficiaries as of the date of disability shall be entitled to receive the monthly pension: Provided, That if he has no primary beneficiaries and he dies within sixty (60) months from the start of his monthly pension, his secondary beneficiaries shall be entitled to a lump sum benefit equivalent to the total monthly pensions corresponding to the balance of the five-year guaranteed period excluding the dependents' pension. (d) The following disabilities shall be deemed permanent total: (1) Complete loss of sight of both eyes; (2) Loss of two limbs at or above the ankle or wrists; (3) Permanent complete paralysis of two limbs; (4) Brain injury resulting to incurable imbecility or insanity; and (5) Such cases as determined and approved by the SSS. (e) If the disability is permanent partial, and such disability occurs before thirty-six (36) monthly contributions have been paid prior to the semester of disability, the benefit shall be such percentage of the lump sum benefit described in the preceding paragraph with due regard to the degree of disability as the Commission may determine. (f) If the disability is permanent partial and such disability occurs after thirty-six (36) monthly contributions have been paid prior to the semester of disability, the benefit shall be the monthly pension for permanent total disability payable not longer than the period designated in the following schedule: one thumb 10 months; one index finger 8; one middle finger 6; one ring finger 5; one little finger 3; one big toe 6; one hand 39; one arm 50; one foot 31; one leg 46; one ear 10; both ears 20; hearing of one ear 10; hearing of both ears 50; sight of one eye 25. (g) The percentage degree of disability which is equivalent to the ratio that the designated number of months of compensability bears to seventy-five (75), rounded to the next higher integer, shall not be additive for distinct, separate and unrelated permanent partial disabilities, but shall be additive for deteriorating and related permanent partial disabilities, to a maximum of one hundred percent (100%), in which case, the member shall be deemed as permanently totally disabled. (h) In case of permanent partial disability, the monthly pension benefit shall be given in lump sum if it is payable for less than twelve (12) months. (i) For the purpose of adjudicating retirement, death and permanent total disability pension benefits, contributions shall be deemed paid for the months during which the member received partial disability pension: Provided, That such contributions shall be based on his last contribution prior to his disability. (j) Should a member who is on partial disability pension retire or die, his disability pension shall cease upon his retirement or death.
provisions.explanation: Disability mirrors death's 36-contribution line: permanent total disability with 36+ contributions earns the monthly pension (plus dependents' pension); below 36, a lump sum of (pension × contributions) or 12× pension, higher. A lump-sum recipient who returns to work at least one year after disability re-enters compulsory coverage as a new member. The pension suspends on reemployment, recovery, or skipping the annual SSS medical exam. Death of a disability pensioner follows the same 60-month survivor rule as retirees. Permanent total disabilities are the five listed cases (both eyes, two limbs, two-limb paralysis, brain injury causing incurable imbecility/insanity, SSS-approved cases). Permanent partial disability uses the statutory schedule (months of pension per body part, e.g. one arm 50, one leg 46, one hand 39, sight of one eye 25); the degree (months ÷ 75, rounded up) aggregates only for deteriorating and related disabilities up to 100%, which converts the case to permanent total. Schedule awards under 12 months are paid in lump sum; months on partial disability pension count as paid contributions (at the last rate) toward later retirement/death/PTD claims; and the partial pension stops on retirement or death. Ortega v. SSC is the companion case: total permanent disability is adjudicated on SSS medical findings and substantial evidence, and SSS benefits are conceptually distinct from Labor Code compensation. Remember: 36/12× structure parallels Sec. 13 exactly.

provisions.verbatim: Funeral Benefit. — A funeral grant equivalent to Twelve thousand pesos (P12,000.00) shall be paid, in cash or in kind, to help defray the cost of funeral expenses upon the death of a member, including permanently totally disabled member or retiree.
provisions.explanation: The statute sets a P12,000 funeral grant payable on the death of any member, including a permanent-total-disability pensioner or retiree. CURRENT RULE (supersedes the peso amount): under SSS Circular No. 2023-009, effective 20 October 2023, the benefit is variable from P20,000 to P60,000 where the member paid at least 36 contributions (scaled to contributions and AMSC), and fixed at P12,000 where the member paid at least 1 but fewer than 36. It is paid to whoever proves the funeral expense (claimant files online via My.SSS if an SSS member, over the counter otherwise). Practical application: funeral claims are the fastest SSS death-related payout and are separate from — and additional to — death benefits under Sec. 13. Exam point: always pair the statutory P12,000 with the Circular 2023-009 update; a question asking the 'current' amount wants P20,000–P60,000/P12,000.
